    pi=[1,1]
    c=2
    objective=sum(pi)+o1+(c-1)*max(*pi,o1)

strengths: Jointly selecting pipeline placement and per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP strategies addresses an important practical problem. The application to ViT and Swin makes this systems contribution relevant to computer vision.

Table 1 reports meaningful measured gains: on ENVB-8, ViT throughput increases to 45.58 samples/s versus 38.74 for Alpa and 32.20 for Galvatron; Swin reaches 19.08 versus 13.90 for Galvatron. Llama-7B achieves the reported 3.80× improvement on ENVC.

Automation provides value even when throughput matches a baseline. For BERT on ENVA, search takes 0.37 minutes versus Galvatron's 6.44 minutes. On ENVD-32, UniAP matches the fastest enumerated Megatron configurations while substantially reducing search time.

Evaluation spans several hardware platforms, with additional weak-scaling results up to 64 DCUs. The appendices provide model configurations, solver settings, an interpretable placement case study, and encouraging throughput-estimation accuracy on selected strategies.
weaknesses: The stated constraints do not ensure correctly ordered pipeline stages. For a two-layer graph u -> v, assigning u to stage 2 and v to stage 1 satisfies the contiguity and placement constraints, but Equation (4) assigns zero communication cost to the dependency. The objective can therefore favor placements that omit required communication costs. This directly undermines the central formulation and is the principal reason the balance favors rejection despite the useful measurements.

Equations (3) and (4) contain fourth-degree products of decision variables, such as P_ui P_vi S_uk S_vl, rather than a quadratic formulation. Auxiliary-variable reformulations are possible, but none is supplied. Consequently, the actual solver-ready formulation and its relationship to the reported implementation cannot be reconstructed from the manuscript.

The repeated optimality claims exceed the evidence. Appendix E imposes a 60-second limit and permits termination after 15 seconds with a gap below 4%, but achieved gaps and timeout frequencies are unreported. Section 3.5 bounds a time-budgeted procedure; it does not establish the stated complexity for obtaining an optimal solution. Moreover, optimality under estimated costs would not establish optimal measured throughput.

Memory feasibility is insufficiently specified for the chosen GPipe schedule. Algorithm 1 passes micro-batch size b = B/c to cost modeling, while Section 3.2 scales activation memory by batch size and Equation (5) contains no explicit accumulation across the c retained micro-batches. The manuscript does not explain how this is reconciled or validate predicted peak memory. Appendix F evaluates throughput estimates only for selected strategies, which does not establish memory-model correctness or candidate-ranking accuracy.

The ablation does not isolate the central advantage claimed over hierarchical optimization. Figure 6 compares joint search against inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only search, rather than hierarchical search using the same candidate space and cost model. Hierarchical decomposition does not inherently imply suboptimality when its outer search and inner optimization are exhaustive. Differences in cost models and candidate selection therefore remain alternative explanations for the observed gains.

The search-time comparisons have practical scope limitations: UniAP timing covers UOP and excludes preceding profiling, while Section 4.2 attributes substantial speedups to multithreaded Gurobi versus single-threaded baselines. These are useful measured implementation gains, but matched-resource and end-to-end measurements are needed to establish the broader optimization-efficiency claim.
